content.title: Apollo Epithets | Cultures, Examples & Summary - Lesson | Study.com
content.text: Deities in Greek religion had many different epithets, which reflected the different qualities, duties, and roles ascribed to the deity. Apollo has many different epithets in Greek, though relatively few of these appear in Latin literature. Apollo's epithets refer to his aspect as a sun deity, to his origin and birth, to places where he was worshiped, to his function as protector and healer, his relationship to prophecy, truth, and music, to his skill at archery, and his appearance.GreekApollo's most widely used epithet was Phoebus, meaning shining, pure, or bright. What is Apollo's Roman name? The epithet Phoebus was used by both the Greeks and Romans to refer to Apollo in his role as the God of the Sun. This title was used in several distinguished ancient texts, including Homer's Iliad and Virgil's Aeneid. Some ancient authors, such as Aeschylus, believed that the epithet Phoebus was derived from Apollo's grandmother, Phoebe. In the 5th century BCE, Apollo became increasingly identified with Helios (the Sun) by the Greeks. However, in Latin poetry, Apollo the Roman was not conflated with Sol (the Latin sun deity) until the 1st century CE, remaining a distinct deity in literary works until the 5th century CE.One of the most famous epithets of Apollo is Lyceius. Scholars do not agree on the meaning of this epithet, as some believe it means wolf-slayer, some translate it as the giver of light, and others again believe it refers to Apollo's origin in the country of Lycia. Each of these interpretations can be supported by ancient textual sources, however, in most cases this title is used alongside traditions related to wolves and refers to Apollo in his aspect as the destroyer. For example, it was said that wolves protected Apollo's treasures, and that near the altar of Apollo's temple at Delphi was an iron statue of a wolf. Plutarch uses the epithet Lyceius when he notes how a wolf's attack on a herd of cattle catalyzed the worship of Apollo at Argos. Pausanias uses the epithet when explaining that the Syconians believed Apollo had taught them how to get rid of wolves.
